newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Trade envoys scrap over key policy declaration.
newsitem.headline: Trade envoys scrap over key policy declaration.

text.p: Envoys to the World Trade Organisation battled on Friday over the text of a key declaration to be issued by ministers next month on the global trade agenda into the 21st century.

Argument centred on a draft of the document proposed by WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero which includes reference to the controversial issues of linking labour standards and trade and, investment and competition policies.

"There is little sign of compromise at the moment," said one trade diplomat as an informal meeting of heads of delegation of the 125 WTO member countries to try to finalise a text got under way at the two-year-old body's Geneva headquarters.

Major developing countries have said they cannot accept the so-called "new issues", arguing that the bid to include them in a WTO work programme for the next few years is part of a Western effort to sap their national economic strength.

But the United States is pushing very hard for formal acceptance that the labour issue must be handled within the WTO, the European Union wants an accord on competition policy and Japan and Canada, backed by the EU, seek a deal on investment.
The declaration, originally due to have been completed two weeks ago, is to be issued at the end of the WTO's first conference of member countries' trade ministers in Singapore from December 9-13.
But agreement before then on a final text, trade envoys say, now looks highly unlikely and could be left to the ministers themselves to finesse a document that all can accept.

The text submitted on Friday by Ruggiero, a former Italian trade minister who has campaigned for better treatment of the world's poorest countries by the big trading powers, clearly sought to find a mean between bitterly opposing views on the labour issue.

It proposes that the ministers declare they "renew our commitment to the observance of core labour standards and our support for the work of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) in promoting these standards."

Emerging economies, who see the bid to link labour standards with trade through enforceable WTO rules as aimed at hitting the advantage they have FROM lower labour costs, also want to keep the issue in the United Nations agency.

The Ruggiero draft would also have the ministers say that "the contribution the WTO can make to the promotion of such standards is through increased adherence to the rule-based system, together with further trade liberalisation and the economic growth fostered by icreased trade."
"We agree that protectionist measures should not be used to enforce labour standards, and that the competitive advantage of low-wage countries should not be put into question," it adds.

Trade analysts said this formulation was unlikely to go far enough to satisfy the United States -- or international trade union organisations who will be sending their leaders to Singapore -- but could also displease developing countries.

In a phrasing that emerging economies are also resisting, the text would have the ministers azgree to "begin an examination of the relationship between trade and investment" with an eventual report to the WTO'r ruling General Council.

It also has the ministers agree to set up an experts group to study the relationship between competition policy and the WTO and "identify any problems that may require action in the WTO framework...."
Emerging economies fear that any discussion, once begun, would lead to formulation of rules that would prevent them following policies aimed at national industrial development.
